equivalence_validation.candidate_operation: int32 in -> native function -> increment -> int32 out (native.c / napi_addon.c both implement exactly `return x + 1;` as the native-side logic; napi_addon.c additionally performs the N-API-mandated argument/return marshaling calls napi_get_value_int32/napi_create_int32, which is inherent to what the N-API mechanism itself is).
equivalence_validation.argument_type: int32 for bun:ffi, Node/Bun N-API, and Deno Fast-API variant. int64 (BigInt) for Deno's deliberate non-fast variant only (documented, not conflated with the i32 rows for magnitude comparison).
equivalence_validation.return_type: Matches argument type per variant (see above).
equivalence_validation.native_function_body: Byte-for-byte identical `return x + 1;` in the FFI shared library (native.c) used by bun:ffi and both Deno variants. The N-API addon (napi_addon.c) implements the same logical operation, with N-API's own required marshaling calls around it — this is the intended object of measurement for the N-API rows (N-API's own overhead is part of what N-API 'is'), not a departure from equivalence.
equivalence_validation.js_call_structure: Identical for-loop / sink=fn(i) pattern across every variant's script (see benchmark/*.js), differing only in the import/setup lines needed for each binding mechanism.
equivalence_validation.optimization_barriers: sink accumulator, printed in the final JSON output (equivalent to Section 6's console.log(sink) requirement) — prevents the loop/call from being eliminated as dead code. Verified: final sink values in every run's raw data are non-zero and consistent with the expected computation, confirming the loop and the native call actually executed the requested iteration count.
equivalence_validation.allocation_behavior: bun:ffi and Deno.dlopen() marshal int32/int64 arguments directly (no heap allocation for primitive numeric FFI calls, consistent with both runtimes' FFI documentation). N-API's napi_create_int32 return-value boxing may or may not allocate depending on each engine's small-integer (SMI-style) tagging — this was NOT independently verified at the engine-internals level this session and is disclosed as an open uncertainty, not asserted as zero-allocation.
equivalence_validation.exception_behavior: None of the four variants throw during normal operation; error paths (e.g. napi_get_value_int32 failing on a non-number argument) are never exercised, since every call always passes a valid int32/int64.
equivalence_validation.thread_async_behavior: All four variants are fully synchronous, single-threaded, same-thread calls — no cross-thread hop (unlike H2's fetch() thread-hop test). Deno's dlopen symbols were declared without `nonblocking: true` (the default, synchronous dispatch), confirmed by reading the symbol definitions in deno-ffi-bench.js.
equivalence_validation.conclusion: True three-way apples-to-apples equivalence (identical binding technology for all three runtimes) was NOT achievable — Node has no built-in dlopen-style FFI without a third-party package, and Deno has no N-API/native-addon compatibility. Per Section 4, this experiment therefore uses: PRIMARY COMPARISON = Bun's own normal binding (bun:ffi) vs Node's own normal/actual binding (N-API addon) — the fairest 'each runtime's real native-call path' comparison. SUPPLEMENTARY SAME-BINARY CONTROL = the identical compiled napi_addon.node loaded by both Bun (via its N-API compat layer) and Node (natively) — the strongest possible equivalence for isolating engine-level differences, at the cost of testing Bun's N-API EMULATION overhead rather than Bun's fastest normal path. DENO = presented separately, explicitly NOT APPLES-TO-APPLES against the N-API rows (different FFI technology), with two internally-comparable sub-variants (fast/non-fast) and a loosely-comparable relationship to bun:ffi as both are dlopen-based FFI systems (though even this is not asserted as fully equivalent, since bun:ffi's and Deno's FFI internal implementations were not independently source-verified against each other this session).

background_workload.description: Shared cloud sandbox; same session-management processes present as in prior experiments (roughly constant, low CPU usage). No HTTP load generator, database, or other benchmark running concurrently.

timer_resolution_note: Timing uses process.hrtime.bigint() (nanosecond-resolution counter), chunked over 1,000,000 calls per chunk (10 chunks per 10,000,000-call timed run) so the timer call itself (invoked only 20 times per run, not once per native call) is amortized to a negligible fraction of the measured time — satisfying Section 8's 'remove the timer from the result' requirement. Control-mode measurements (pure JS loop, no native call) show notably higher relative variance (CV 25%-37%) than test-mode measurements (CV 3.6%-6.3%) because the ABSOLUTE per-call cost being measured in control mode (~0.45-0.9ns) is extremely close to the practical noise floor of what a chunked, non-hardware-performance-counter timing approach can resolve on shared, non-isolated cores — this is disclosed rather than hidden; the derived 'native-call overhead' figures (test minus control) are still meaningful because the test-mode absolute magnitudes (5-82ns) are far above this noise floor, so the control's relative imprecision contributes only a small fraction of the subtracted overhead's own uncertainty.
